comparison: Perfect alignment on masking experiment findings (C73-C81). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED that masking effects and intensity variations demonstrate auditory-driven inhibition. OpenEval notes authors acknowledge alternative interpretations (C84), while peer reviewers do not challenge the findings and view masking as a study strength.

Strong disagreement on dose-response findings (C44-C48, C96). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED that no dose-response relationship exists, citing null findings across experiments. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 explicitly challenging the conclusion, noting point estimates suggest 'a more complex picture' and that 'the present data and analyses cannot rule out that there is a dose-response function.'

Full agreement on masking effectiveness (C59-C63). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED that masking did not unmask hidden neuromodulatory effects and that auditory differences between sites were not obscuring direct effects. Peer reviewers cite masking as a study strength without raising concerns.

Complete agreement on auditory stimulus characteristics (C65-C72). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED that stimulus duration and pitch affect MEP inhibition regardless of TUS administration. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm that acoustic stimulation explains MEP suppression, encompassing these auditory parameter findings.

Perfect alignment on uncertainty (C53-C57, C106). Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN the exploratory finding of potential direct neuromodulation under specific conditions. OpenEval notes authors explicitly state this is preliminary requiring further work. Peer reviewers do not comment on this exploratory result, and it is absent from editor's summary.

Strong agreement on MEP suppression across all conditions (C34-C43, C102, C104, C105). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes lack of spatial specificity and equivalent sham effects. Peer review (R1) incorporates these claims into broader affirmation of the core auditory confound finding, with all reviewers explicitly affirming the evidence.

Full agreement on primary conclusion (C8, C9, C32, C85, C94-C96, C105, C107, C149). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED that observed effects are due to auditory confounds rather than direct neuromodulation. Editor states study 'provides convincing evidence' and all reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding with converging evidence from multiple experiments.

Strong agreement on methodological critiques and recommendations (C11-C13, C27, C100, C138-C139, C147, C151). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes that prior controls were insufficient and recommendations logically follow. Peer reviewers strongly support these conclusions, with editor noting findings 'lay the ground for future studies' and reviewers praising the study's impact.

Agreement on learning mechanism interpretation (C89-C93, C118). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED that trial-by-trial patterns indicate expectation-based inhibition rather than habituation. OpenEval notes interpretation is somewhat speculative. Peer reviewers do not challenge this mechanistic interpretation, and editor's affirmation of auditory confound implicitly supports the proposed mechanism.

Strong agreement on future study recommendations (C140-C146). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED that recommendations are practical and well-justified. Peer review (R9) strongly supports these, with Reviewer 1 suggesting specific methods (smoothed ramped US wave) and Reviewer 2 confirming study will impact the field.

Agreement on contextualizing findings (C136-C137). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED the distinction that null findings apply to specific protocols, not all TUS applications. Peer review (R10) supports this nuanced conclusion, with editor framing findings as groundwork for optimization rather than dismissal of TUS.

Agreement on limitations and alternative interpretations (C135 shared, plus C124-C133 in OpenEval only). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED that authors appropriately acknowledge limitations. OpenEval emphasizes balanced discussion of null findings not generalizing to all parameters. Peer reviewers accept the nuanced framing without challenging limitations discussion.

OpenEval addresses methodological approach details (C152-C163) rating as SUPPORTED the multi-center design, sample sizes, and use of established protocols. Peer review (R8) praises experimental design broadly (C5-C7, C28-C31), with all reviewers emphasizing 'remarkable efforts' and 'multitude of control conditions' as study strengths. Overlapping positive assessment of methodology.

OpenEval evaluates specific experimental designs (C164-C177) as SUPPORTED, highlighting preregistration, simulations, and blinding. Peer review (R8) provides broader affirmation of experimental design quality, with editor and reviewers praising control conditions and efforts to isolate confounds. Both strongly positive on methodological rigor.

OpenEval rates Experiment III design (C178-C183) as SUPPORTED for isolating auditory effects. Peer review (R8) does not separately evaluate this experiment but includes it in overall praise of 'multitude of control conditions' and 'remarkable efforts' to control confounds. Implicit agreement on methodological soundness.

OpenEval rates Experiment IV design (C184-C191) as SUPPORTED for testing audibility hypothesis, noting authors acknowledge additional controls would strengthen inferences. Peer review (R8) praises overall experimental design without separately addressing this experiment. Implicit agreement on approach with acknowledged limitations.

OpenEval evaluates statistical analysis methods (C192-C195) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate transformation, LMM approach, and visual confirmation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found that specifically addresses statistical methodology, though overall positive reception implies acceptance of analytical approach.
